q-ar-ain.label: a or an
q-ar-ain.summary: The choice follows the sound the next word starts with, not its spelling.

q-ar-the.label: When 'the' is needed
q-ar-the.summary: Superlatives, one-of-a-kind things, rivers, ranges, oceans and ordinals take 'the'.

q-ar-none.label: Where no article belongs
q-ar-none.summary: Abstract and uncountable nouns in general, meals, languages, and most proper nouns take none.

q-ar-idiom.label: Idiomatic phrases with/without an article
q-ar-idiom.summary: A set group of phrases always carries 'a' (make a noise, tell a lie) and a separate set always carries none (at home, by mistake).

q-ar-plural.label: a/an with plurals and uncountables
q-ar-plural.summary: 'A/an' never goes before a plural noun, and an uncountable noun needs a measure word (a piece of, a slice of) before it can take 'a'.

q-ar-exception.label: Unique-sounding nouns that take no 'the'
q-ar-exception.summary: Heaven, Hell, God and Parliament sound one-of-a-kind but take no article, and a monument named after a person or place drops 'the' too.

q-ar-manysuch.label: 'A/an' after many, such, quite, rather
q-ar-manysuch.summary: Many a, such a, quite a and rather a all take a singular noun even though 'many' and 'such' usually signal a plural idea.

rules.text: Use 'an' before a vowel SOUND and 'a' before a consonant sound. Spelling does not decide it: an hour, an MLA, an honest man; a university, a one-rupee coin, a European.
rules.ok: An hour, a university, an MP.
rules.bad: A hour, an university, a MP.

rules.text: 'The' goes before a superlative, an ordinal, a thing there is only one of, and before rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts and groups of islands. Single mountains and single lakes take none.
rules.ok: The tallest boy, the Ganga, the Himalayas, the sun.
rules.bad: Tallest boy, Ganga is holy, Himalayas are high.

rules.text: 'The' also marks a noun already known from the situation or mentioned before, and it makes a singular noun stand for its whole class: the tiger is disappearing.
rules.ok: I bought a book. The book was torn.
rules.bad: I bought a book. A book was torn.

rules.text: No article before an abstract or uncountable noun used in general (honesty, advice, information, furniture), before meals, languages, games, most diseases, and before a proper noun; add 'the' only when the noun is narrowed down.
rules.ok: Honesty pays. He plays cricket after lunch.
rules.bad: The honesty pays. He plays the cricket after the lunch.

rules.text: In 'the more ... the more' and 'the + adjective' for a whole class (the poor, the blind), 'the' is required. One article serves two nouns of the same person or thing, but two are needed for two different ones.
rules.ok: The more he earns, the less he saves. A black and a white shirt (two shirts).
rules.bad: More he earns, less he saves.

rules.text: A fixed group of phrases always keeps 'a': in a hurry, in a fix, in a nutshell, make a noise, keep a secret, as a rule, at a loss, tell a lie. A separate fixed group never takes an article at all: at home, by mistake, in danger, catch fire, by car/bus, lose heart.
rules.ok: He never tells a lie. The papers caught fire by mistake.
rules.bad: He never tells lie. The papers caught the fire by the mistake.

rules.text: 'A/an' never goes before a plural noun (not 'a boys', just 'boys' or 'the boys'). An uncountable noun (advice, furniture, information, luggage) cannot take 'a' either, unless a measure word turns it countable: a piece of advice, a slice of bread, an item of furniture.
rules.ok: The boys have come. She gave me a piece of advice.
rules.bad: A boys have come. She gave me an advice.

rules.text: Heaven, Hell, God and Parliament sound like one-of-a-kind things but take no article at all. A building or monument whose name already includes a person's or place's name (Delhi Airport, Indira Gandhi Stadium) also drops 'the', even though a plain monument name takes it (the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort).
rules.ok: God resides in heaven. The Bill was passed in Parliament. He landed at Indira Gandhi Airport.
rules.bad: The God resides in the heaven. He landed at the Indira Gandhi Airport.

rules.text: 'Many a', 'such a', 'quite a' and 'rather a' are all followed by a singular noun, not a plural one, even though 'many' and 'such' on their own suggest more than one. The same distributive 'a' also means 'per' after a rate or price: ten rupees a kilo, sixty kilometres an hour.
rules.ok: Many a student has failed this test. This car runs fifteen kilometres a litre.
rules.bad: Many a students have failed this test.

q-ar-ain.cue: A blank before a noun or adjective, with 'a' and 'an' among the options.
q-ar-ain.standard: Say the next word aloud. If it begins with a vowel sound, use 'an'; otherwise 'a'.
q-ar-ain.fast: Test the first sound, not the first letter: h in 'hour' is silent, u in 'university' sounds like 'yoo'.
q-ar-ain.eliminate: Drop 'the' and the blank option first if the noun is being introduced for the first time.
traps: Words beginning with a silent h (hour, honour, heir) take 'an'.
Words beginning with a 'yoo' or 'wun' sound (university, European, one) take 'a'.
Single letters and abbreviations go by sound: an MLA, an FIR, a UPSC notification.

q-ar-the.cue: A blank before a superlative, an ordinal, a river or range, or a noun mentioned earlier.
q-ar-the.standard: Ask whether the noun is one of a kind, already known, or the best or first of something. If yes, use 'the'.
q-ar-the.fast: Superlative or ordinal in the phrase means 'the'.
q-ar-the.eliminate: If the noun is being met for the first time and is countable and singular, 'the' is usually wrong.
traps: Rivers and ranges take 'the' but single peaks and lakes do not.
'The' before a second mention is easy to drop in a long sentence.

q-ar-none.cue: A blank before an abstract noun, a meal, a language or a game, with 'no article' among the options.
q-ar-none.standard: Ask whether the noun is being used in general. If it is, leave it bare.
q-ar-none.fast: Abstract noun used generally, meal, language or game: no article.
q-ar-none.eliminate: Cross out 'the' unless the sentence narrows the noun down with a phrase or clause.
traps: 'Advice', 'information', 'furniture' and 'luggage' are uncountable and take no 'a'.
'The' returns as soon as the noun is specified: the advice he gave me.

q-ar-idiom.cue: A familiar fixed phrase (make a noise, at home, by mistake, catch fire) with the article itself in question.
q-ar-idiom.standard: Recall the phrase as a whole unit rather than reasoning about the noun inside it.
q-ar-idiom.fast: Noise/secret/lie/hurry/fix/loss/rule phrases keep 'a'. Home/mistake/danger/fire/car phrases keep none.
q-ar-idiom.eliminate: Drop 'the' for both groups; these phrases never use 'the'.
traps: 'By mistake' is often wrongly given 'a' or 'the'.
'Catch fire' / 'set on fire' never takes an article even though 'fire' can be a countable event elsewhere.

q-ar-plural.cue: A plural noun or an uncountable noun (advice, furniture, information) with 'a/an' among the options.
q-ar-plural.standard: Check whether the noun is plural or uncountable first; if either, 'a/an' alone cannot be right.
q-ar-plural.fast: Plural noun: no 'a'. Uncountable noun: no 'a' unless a measure word (piece/slice/item of) comes first.
q-ar-plural.eliminate: Drop any option that puts 'a/an' directly before a plural or an uncountable noun with no measure word.
traps: 'Advice', 'information', 'furniture', 'luggage' feel countable in translation but are not in English.
'A boys have come' is ungrammatical in two ways: the article and the verb.

q-ar-exception.cue: Heaven, Hell, God, Parliament, or a monument whose name already contains a person's or place's name.
q-ar-exception.standard: Check whether the proper noun already has a person's or institution's name built in; if so, no 'the', even though it names something unique.
q-ar-exception.fast: Heaven/Hell/God/Parliament: never 'the'. Name + Airport/Stadium/Palace (a person or place already in it): never 'the'. Bare monument name: 'the'.
q-ar-exception.eliminate: Drop 'the' before Heaven, Hell, God and Parliament on sight.
traps: 'The Taj Mahal' takes 'the' but 'Indira Gandhi Airport' does not, even though both are unique.
'Go to hell' and 'in heaven' never take 'the' despite sounding like unique places.

q-ar-manysuch.cue: 'Many', 'such', 'quite' or 'rather' directly before a noun, or a rate/price phrase ('a litre', 'an hour').
q-ar-manysuch.standard: After many/such/quite/rather, keep the noun singular and insert 'a/an' between the word and the noun.
q-ar-manysuch.fast: Many a + singular noun. Such a + singular noun. Rate per unit: a/an also means 'per'.
q-ar-manysuch.eliminate: Drop any option that pluralises the noun after 'many a' or 'such a'.
traps: 'Many a student' takes a singular verb too: 'has', not 'have'.
'Rather a pity' and 'quite an impossible task' keep the indefinite article even though 'quite' and 'rather' are adverbs of degree.

pyqs.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
No sooner did the Commissioner enter the hall / than the members rose from their seats / and greeted him with a loud applause.
options: No sooner did the Commissioner enter the hall
than the members rose from their seats
and greeted him with a loud applause
pyqs.why: 'Applause' is an uncountable noun and cannot take 'a'; the correct phrase is simply 'with loud applause'. The 'no sooner ... than' inversion in the first two parts is correctly formed.

a.note: The inversion after 'no sooner' is correctly formed: did + subject + base verb.

b.note: 'Than the members rose' correctly completes the 'no sooner ... than' pair.

d.note: There is an error, in part (c).

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The meeting lasted ___ hour and a half.
practice.why: 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes 'an'.

a.note: 'A hour' goes by the letter h instead of the sound; the h in 'hour' is not pronounced.

c.note: 'The hour' would point to one particular hour already known, which the sentence does not.

d.note: A singular countable noun being introduced needs an article.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
She has joined ___ university in Pune.
practice.why: 'University' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes 'a'.

a.note: 'An university' goes by the vowel letter u; the word is pronounced 'yoo-niversity'.

c.note: 'The university' would mean a particular one already known to the listener.

d.note: A singular countable noun needs an article here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He filed ___ FIR at the police station.
practice.why: The abbreviation FIR is read as 'ef-eye-ar', which begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

a.note: 'A FIR' goes by the letter F; read aloud, the letter begins with the vowel sound 'ef'.

c.note: 'The FIR' would refer to one already mentioned; here it is being filed for the first time.

d.note: A singular countable noun needs an article here.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He is ___ tallest boy in the class.
practice.why: A superlative singles out one person, so it takes 'the'.

a.note: 'A tallest' is impossible: a superlative cannot be one of several.

b.note: 'An tallest' is wrong in both the article and the sound.

d.note: Leaving out the article before a superlative is a common slip; English requires 'the'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
___ Ganga rises in the Himalayas.
practice.why: Rivers take 'the', as do mountain ranges, seas and oceans.

a.note: 'A Ganga' would make the river one of several of that name.

b.note: 'An Ganga' is wrong in both the article and the sound.

d.note: Dropping the article before a river name is common in speech, but a river takes 'the'.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
I bought a dictionary yesterday / but dictionary was missing / twenty pages / in the middle.
practice.why: At the second mention the noun is already known, so it needs 'the dictionary'.

a.note: 'A dictionary' is right for the first mention of a countable noun.

c.note: 'Twenty pages' is a plural count and needs no article.

d.note: 'In the middle' is a fixed phrase and is correct.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
___ honesty is the best policy in the long run.
practice.why: An abstract noun used in general takes no article.

a.note: 'A honesty' is impossible: honesty is uncountable.

b.note: 'An honesty' is impossible for the same reason.

c.note: 'The honesty' would point to one particular person's honesty, which the sentence does not do.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
He gave me / a very useful advice / about the examination / last evening.
practice.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'a'; it should be 'very useful advice' or 'a very useful piece of advice'.

a.note: 'He gave me' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'About the examination' points to a known examination and is correct.

d.note: 'Last evening' is a correct phrase of time.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
[[The more you read the more]] you understand.
options: The more you read, the more
practice.why: Both halves of the 'the more ... the more' pattern keep 'the'.

b.note: Dropping both articles is the commonest form of this error; the pattern needs 'the' twice.

c.note: The second half has lost its 'the'.

d.note: The first half has lost its 'the'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
We had ___ lunch at a small place near the office.
practice.why: Names of meals take no article when they mean the meal in general.

a.note: 'A lunch' is used only when the meal is described as an event, as in 'a lunch in his honour'.

b.note: 'The lunch' would point to one particular meal already known.

d.note: 'An lunch' is wrong in both the article and the sound.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The watchman was dismissed for sleeping ___ duty and failing to raise an alarm.
practice.why: 'On duty' is a fixed phrase that takes no article at all; the blank here is a preposition slot, not an article slot, so none of the article options fit.

b.note: 'In a duty' forces an article into a fixed phrase that never takes one.

c.note: 'A duty' alone does not complete the fixed expression 'on duty'.

d.note: 'The duty' would need a different sentence structure naming which duty.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
He was in such / a hurry that he / set the house on / a fire by mistake.
practice.why: 'Set on fire' and 'by mistake' are both fixed phrases that take no article; the correct ending is 'set the house on fire by mistake'.

a.note: 'In such a hurry' is a correct fixed phrase with 'a'.

b.note: A correct continuation of the 'in such a hurry' phrase.

c.note: 'Set the house on' correctly leads into the fixed phrase 'on fire'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
Do not worry, I will keep [[the secret]] you told me.
practice.why: 'Keep a secret' is the fixed phrase; 'the secret' wrongly treats this as a particular, already-known secret rather than the general act of keeping one.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: Dropping the article entirely breaks the fixed phrase, which always keeps 'a'.

d.note: 'Secret' begins with a consonant sound, so 'an' is also wrong.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The manager gave / an useful advices / to all the / new employees yesterday.
practice.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'an' or a plural '-s'; it should read 'useful advice' or 'a useful piece of advice'.

a.note: 'The manager gave' is a correct opening.

c.note: 'To all the' is a correct continuation.

d.note: 'New employees yesterday' is a correct closing phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I need ___ information about the new admission process.
practice.why: 'Information' is uncountable and cannot take 'a' directly; a measure phrase like 'a piece of' makes it countable, though plain 'some' would also work without an article.

a.note: 'An information' puts the indefinite article directly before an uncountable noun, which is never allowed.

c.note: 'The information' would mean one specific, already-known set of information, which the sentence does not establish.

d.note: 'Some information' is grammatical but is not the option this question is testing: the measure-word pattern with 'a'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The new metro line passes close to ___ Indira Gandhi Airport.
practice.why: A monument or building whose name already contains a person's name drops 'the', even though it is a unique place.

a.note: Adding 'the' before a proper noun that already carries a person's name is a common over-correction.

b.note: 'An' does not fit the consonant sound at the start of 'Indira'.

c.note: 'A' would make the airport one of several, which is not the meaning here.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
After his death, / everyone believed / he had gone to / the heaven peacefully.
practice.why: 'Heaven' never takes an article despite sounding like a unique place; the correct ending is 'he had gone to heaven peacefully'.

a.note: 'After his death,' is a correct opening clause.

c.note: 'He had gone to' is a correct lead-in to the fixed phrase.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
___ citizen has questioned the sudden rise in fuel prices this month.
practice.why: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb, even though the overall meaning is plural.

b.note: Plain 'many' needs a plural noun ('many citizens'), not a singular one.

c.note: 'Many of' needs a determiner before the noun ('many of the citizens').

d.note: 'A many' reverses the fixed word order; the correct form is 'many a'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
It was [[quite impossible task]] to finish the report overnight.
practice.why: 'Quite' before a singular countable noun still needs the indefinite article, and 'impossible' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

b.note: This repeats the original error unchanged.

c.note: 'Impossible' begins with a vowel sound, so 'a' is the wrong form of the article here.

d.note: 'The impossible task' would mean one particular, already-known task rather than describing how hard the task was.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This bike gives a mileage of about fifty kilometres ___ litre.
practice.why: The indefinite article can mean 'per' after a rate: fifty kilometres a litre, ten rupees a kilo.

b.note: 'Litre' begins with a consonant sound, so 'an' does not fit.

c.note: 'The litre' would point to one specific, already-known litre, not a general rate.

d.note: 'Per a' doubles up two words that both mean 'per'; only one is needed.
